<reason>Side A controlled the terms of the motion as written: the tie between coverage and work status. A's sharpest line—that CON's subsidized-continuation "repair" is public financing for exactly the costliest populations private coverage abandons—put B on the defensive, and B's "exclusivity is the distinction" reply, while coherent, never fully explained why non-exclusive public financing plus duplicate private administration is preferable rather than merely familiar. B scored real points: the symmetry argument (if political reform can fix single-payer underfunding, it can finance continuity) and the concession-forcing observation that A's "campaignable" queue does not produce an appointment. B also honestly conceded that individual patients lack exit in employer plans, which damaged its pluralism route. But A absorbed the queue pressure better than B absorbed the principled-line pressure, and A's closing crystallized the decision rule ("residence beats payroll") more memorably than B's closing crystallized concentration risk. Both sides followed format (proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure), stayed grounded without fake citations, and narrowed the clash over rounds. A wins clear but competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was A's backstop trap: CON's continuity fix publicly finances the sick and unemployed—the exact population private plans find costliest—so the "principled line" question (A3.2) forced B to rest everything on the exclusivity/pluralism distinction. B's A2 answer and closing defended that distinction competently, but A's framing ("a second roof built over a leaking one, at full price") made the redundancy of the patched system vivid, and B's own concession that no individual exit is guaranteed left the pluralism benefit resting on employer interests rather than patient interests.</best_rebuttal>
